atlas-my.0001: A study destination with a hard step to work: students may only work in term breaks, in a short list of jobs, and a graduate needs an Employment Pass whose minimum basic salary rose to RM5,000 a month on 1 June 2026. Kuala Lumpur, the capital, is the second-largest contributor to the economy after Selangor.
atlas-my.0004: The capital and services economy, where foreign banks have their Malaysian head offices
atlas-my.0005: licensed commercial bank, head office in Kuala Lumpur
atlas-my.0007: Malaysia was not covered by the research library before this record.
atlas-my.0008: Malaysia visas, Employment Pass salary tiers, EMGS student routes and entry rules are fully verified in visas_immigration/malaysia/malaysia_visas_immigration_guide.md.
atlas-my.0009: No source read gives Kuala Lumpur’s jobs by sector, so its finance rating rests on named banks’ head offices, not a statistic.
atlas-my.0010: Entry for EU passports, graduate pay, tax and language expectations were not researched.
atlas-my.0011: From 1 June 2026 the lowest Employment Pass category needs a basic salary of at least RM5,000 a month (up from RM3,000) and lasts up to 5 years, with a succession plan; the higher categories start at RM10,000 and RM20,000.
atlas-my.0012: Kuala Lumpur’s economy grew 5.2% in 2025 to RM265.1 billion; as the capital it remained the second-largest contributor to Malaysia’s economy after Selangor, and services made up more than 90% of it, with finance, insurance, real estate and business services growing 5.3%.
atlas-my.0013: Deutsche Bank (Malaysia) Berhad is a licensed commercial bank with its office on Jalan Sultan Ismail, Kuala Lumpur.
atlas-my.0014: Bank of America Malaysia Berhad is a licensed commercial bank and principal dealer with its office in Menara Merdeka 118, Kuala Lumpur.
atlas-my.0015: The UK Foreign Office advises against all but essential travel to the islands and dive sites off eastern Sabah, from Sandakan to Tawau, because of the threat of kidnapping; this does not apply to mainland Sabah.
atlas-my.0016: Malaysia’s electrical and electronics manufacturing hub
atlas-my.0019: The state across from Singapore, Malaysia’s data-centre and digital-economy hub
atlas-my.0021: Pulau Pinang’s economy grew 7.3% in 2025 to RM130.3 billion, led by electrical, electronic and optical products, up 12.7%; the statistics office calls it Malaysia’s leading electrical and electronics hub.
atlas-my.0022: Johor grew fastest of all states in 2025, by 8.0% to RM171 billion, nearly 10% of Malaysia’s economy, driven by data centres; the statistics office calls it the nation’s digital economy hub.
atlas-my.0023: Penang’s IT rating rests on one employer’s design and shared-services functions: the statistics office describes its electronics manufacturing, not graduate hiring by role. Johor’s IT rating rests on data-centre growth, which creates more construction and operations jobs than graduate IT roles.
atlas-my.0024: The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Kuala Lumpur 39th in the world, up three places, and Labuan 44th.
atlas-my.0025: Startup Genome’s 2026 report puts Kuala Lumpur in the 31–40 range of its emerging ecosystems and 19th in Asia, after it slipped more than 15 places.
atlas-my.0026: CIMB says it has grown from its headquarters in Kuala Lumpur to around 33,000 employees serving over 30 million customers across ASEAN and beyond.
atlas-my.0027: In December 2025 the median monthly wage of formal-sector employees was RM3,167 across Malaysia: RM4,391 in Kuala Lumpur, RM3,500 in Pulau Pinang and RM2,982 in Johor.
atlas-my.0028: Intel Malaysia was established in Penang in 1972 and, in the investment agency’s words, is Intel’s largest and most diverse site outside the United States, covering manufacturing, product design and development and global shared services.
atlas-my.0029: Infineon says its Penang team is in the Phase 2 Bayan Lepas Free Industrial Zone and invites applications to its jobs there.
atlas-my.0030: Micron lists Penang and Muar in Malaysia among its manufacturing locations.
atlas-my.0031: Malaysia recorded RM385.7 billion of data-centre investment from 2021 to the first half of 2026; the investment authority names AWS, Microsoft, Google, Bridge Data Centres, DayOne, AirTrunk and Vantage Data Centres as operators present, particularly in Greater Kuala Lumpur and Johor.
atlas-my.0032: headquartered in Kuala Lumpur; around 33,000 employees
atlas-my.0033: founded in Penang in 1972; manufacturing, design and shared services
atlas-my.0034: Phase 2, Bayan Lepas Free Industrial Zone
atlas-my.0037: AWS, Microsoft, Google and Bridge Data Centres among those named
atlas-my.0038: English is the default language of private-sector and multinational recruiting in Malaysia, while Bahasa Malaysia is sometimes required for government, government-linked and some local or front-line roles.
atlas-my.0039: Graduate windows are mixed rather than one national season: CIMB’s Complete Banker has intakes in April and October, its Protégé takes applications all year round, and the 2026 fairs ran on 25 and 26 July (myStarjob, Johor Bahru) and 1 August (TalentBank, Penang); industrial training placements usually last 3 to 6 months.
atlas-my.0040: In 2024 graduate unemployment was 3.2% (165,900 people), down from 3.4%, with 5.14 million graduates in the labour force; about 67.8% of employed graduates were in skilled occupations, skill-related underemployment was 32.2%, and the median monthly salary was RM4,521.
atlas-my.0041: Malaysian students usually do an industrial training placement before graduating, typically 3 to 6 months, and graduate hiring runs through structured programmes at banks, government-linked groups and the Big Four, many of them limited to Malaysian citizens. Graduate unemployment was 3.2% in 2024, but the entry market is crowded and about a third of graduates work below their skill level.
atlas-my.0043: Industrial training puts students in a company, agency or other organisation for supervised work before they receive a certificate, diploma or bachelor’s degree; it usually lasts 3 to 6 months depending on the institution and programme.
atlas-my.0044: The national Structured Internship Programme (MySIP) of TalentCorp sets a minimum allowance of RM600 a month for bachelor’s-level placements and RM500 for diploma-level ones; government agencies pay RM5 an hour for up to 90 working days.
atlas-my.0045: No conversion rate from placement to job offer was found in the pages read, so this ranking rests on the structure of degrees, not on a survey.
atlas-my.0046: Banks and government-linked investors run the visible schemes: CIMB’s Complete Banker is a 24-month regional programme with intakes in April and October and a minimum CGPA of 3.25, its Protégé programme is 8 months of on-the-job training taking applications all year round, and Khazanah’s Graduate Trainee Programme lasts 12 months with a minimum CGPA of 3.0.
atlas-my.0047: Many are for citizens only: Khazanah’s programme is open to Malaysian citizens, and Maybank’s graduate and trainee schemes are restricted to Malaysian citizens.
atlas-my.0049: The Big Four are a main door for accounting and business graduates, usually asking for a CGPA of about 3.0; KPMG says it takes about 400 graduates a year.
atlas-my.0050: FDM Group Malaysia lists graduate programmes in data engineering, software engineering, business analysis and project management, and technical engineering on SEEK Grad.
atlas-my.0052: The Public Service Commission (SPA) takes applications online through its SPA9 system, requires Malaysian citizenship and sets a probation period of 1 to 3 years for appointments.
atlas-my.0054: Commercial fairs run through the year: the TalentBank Career Fair was on 1 August 2026 in Penang for graduates and experienced professionals, and the myStarjob Fair on 25 and 26 July 2026 in Johor Bahru offered on-the-spot interviews.
atlas-my.0055: Mass hiring happens in manufacturing: about 1,000 people queued for up to 500 vacancies at an Infineon open interview in Melaka, with RM3,500 starting pay for production operators and technicians.
atlas-my.0056: Graduate unemployment was 3.2% in 2024, but about 36% of tertiary-educated workers were in jobs below their skills.
atlas-my.0057: Programme windows are mixed rather than a single national season: CIMB’s Complete Banker has two intakes a year (April and October) and its Protégé takes applications all year round, while Khazanah’s assessments run in stages after applications close.
atlas-my.0058: Maybank’s graduate and trainee schemes are restricted to Malaysian citizens.
atlas-my.0059: CIMB’s Protégé is open to fresh graduates from all disciplines with at least a diploma and is a contract post; its Complete Banker needs a minimum CGPA of 3.25 and runs five stages from an online application to a final interview with the Group Chief People Officer.
atlas-my.0060: Khazanah, the sovereign investor, runs a 12-month Graduate Trainee Programme with an Investments track and a Khazanah track covering strategy, governance, sustainability, legal and research, for citizens who are fresh graduates or in their final year, or who have up to two years of work experience.
atlas-my.0061: Grab opened its seventh R&D centre in Kuala Lumpur and aimed to bring on 100 tech staff in its first year, including software engineers, data scientists and data analysts; the electronics and semiconductor plants of Penang hire engineers, and Intel in Penang employs about 9,000 Malaysians.
atlas-my.0062: The pages read set academic bars by grade, not school: CIMB’s Complete Banker asks for a CGPA of at least 3.25 (second class upper or a WAM of 75), Khazanah for 3.0 (second class upper or a WAM of 70%), and the Big Four typically about 3.0.
